items.finding: The source reports that temperature was varied together with acid concentrations and ionic strength to obtain a robust model.
items.how_it_applies: This suggests treating temperature as a model variable and checking whether the line temperature range needs to be covered in calibration; it does not establish an in-line temperature sensor.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The work concerns lithium recycling liquid-liquid extraction, not a concentrated milk matrix, and the temperature variation was for model building rather than an in-line sensor.

citation.quote: The concentrations of nitric acid and hydrochloric acid as well as the ionic strength and temperature were varied to obtain a robust model.
citation.label: E01 ¶19

items.finding: The source notes that NIR spectra are harder to interpret than conventional methods because absorption bands overlap.
items.how_it_applies: For fat and protein in concentrated milk, this points to overlapping bands and the need for product-specific chemometric calibration and retained laboratory checks; it gives no accuracy figure.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The statement is about NIRS in pharmaceutical unit operations, not a concentrated milk product, and it does not report calibration performance.

citation.quote: However, a disadvantage of NIRS is that it is more difficult to interpret a signal than by using conventional analysis methods, such as chromatography, ultraviolet/visible (UV-VIS) light, and others, because the absorption bands overlap due to spectral complexity.
citation.label: E02 ¶13

items.finding: The source says probe-window contamination from a binder added during the process can make accurate measurement impossible.
items.how_it_applies: This flags window fouling as a risk to watch in the milk line and supports planning cleaning and signal-verification steps; it does not describe long-term fouling or cleaning behaviour for this product.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The contamination example is a pharmaceutical binder, not concentrated milk, and the source does not quantify fouling or cleaning intervals.

citation.quote: However, an accurate measurement may not be possible because of contamination of the probe window due to the addition of a binder during the process, which is a disadvantage.
citation.label: E02 ¶27

items.finding: The source states that the probe housing must be compatible with the installation environment, process chemistry, and sterilization and cleaning protocols across scales.
items.how_it_applies: This could inform a check of housing materials and cleaning compatibility for the line; it is a requirement statement, not evidence of long-term performance.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: It comes from biopharmaceutical Raman probe practice, not NIR in concentrated milk, and does not report fouling or cleaning outcomes.

citation.quote: The first requirement is that the probe housing needs to be compatible with the installation environment, process chemistry, and sterilization and cleaning protocols across multiple scales.
citation.label: E03 ¶23

items.finding: The source describes in-line monitoring as real-time and requiring no sample collection from the process flow.
items.how_it_applies: This supports exploring in-line information for earlier composition changes, but it does not give an achievable response time for this product; a practical comparison should measure it.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The definition is from pharmaceutical unit operations and gives no numeric response time, so transfer to a concentrated milk line is unproven.

citation.quote: In-line is a real time monitoring method using software without collecting a sample from the process flow [121].
citation.label: E02 ¶11
